title: Governor of Nevada

context.text: Incumbent Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is seeking a second term; Nevada limits governors to two terms. He won the June 9 Republican primary with 91.0%.
Attorney General Aaron Ford won the June 9 Democratic primary with 63.8% over Washoe County Commission Chair Alexis Hill.

Only three candidates appear on the November ballot for governor: Lombardo (Republican), Aaron Ford (Democratic) and Danielle Ford, who has no party and qualified by petition. 'None of These Candidates' also appears as a ballot choice in Nevada statewide races.

candidates.name: Joe Lombardo
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 9 Republican primary with 91.0% of the vote.

priorities.text: Education: expanding school choice and accountability, and restoring retention of third graders who are not reading at grade level.
No new taxes, a pledge he has repeated since his first campaign for governor.
Public safety, including a proposal to lower Nevada's felony theft threshold from $1,200 to $750.

positions.summary: Has pushed to expand the state's Opportunity Scholarship program for private-school scholarships, so far blocked by Democrats, and has advanced charter school growth.

His campaign did not say whether the right to an abortion through 24 weeks should be added to the state constitution; he has said he would personally support a 15-week cutoff, but that abortion rights are codified in state law and should be left to voters.

record.text: Reported that he received 605 bills after the 2025 legislative session, signing 518 into law and vetoing 87.
Reinstated Nevada's third-grade reading retention policy as part of his 2023 education omnibus bill, AB400.
Vetoed a 2023 bill to cap corporate ownership of single-family homes, and later reportedly blocked a 2025 effort with stricter limits.
Publicly and financially supported the 2024 ballot question to require voter ID, which passed and needs approval again in 2026.

candidates.name: Aaron Ford
candidates.ballotNote: Won the June 9 Democratic primary with 63.8% over Washoe County Commission Chair Alexis Hill.

priorities.text: Housing affordability: easing permitting, using vacant land, and limiting corporate investors buying single-family homes.
Making data centers pay for their own power and infrastructure and ending tax breaks until they meet commitments.
Raising K-12 funding toward the national average without new taxes, and repealing Nevada's right-to-work law.

positions.summary: Says that as governor he will keep Nevada a firewall on abortion access, IVF and private medical decisions; The Nevada Independent lists him as answering yes on enshrining the right to an abortion through 24 weeks in the state constitution.
positions.quote: ensure that Nevada itself remains a firewall, not just in name, but in practice … that means protecting abortion access, safeguarding IVF, keeping politicians out of private medical decisions.

positions.summary: As attorney general, defended Nevada's 2021 ghost-gun ban in court and sued over machine-gun conversion devices.

record.text: Applauded a unanimous Nevada Supreme Court decision upholding the state's ban on 'ghost guns' (Assembly Bill 286 of 2021) against a vagueness challenge.

Announced that, following his lawsuit alongside a coalition of 16 attorneys general, the Trump administration committed to carving Nevada out of its plan to distribute machine-gun conversion devices, and the ATF told the court it would not return forced reset triggers into the plaintiff states.
As attorney general, testified in support of 2019 criminal-justice reform bill AB236, which raised the felony theft threshold from $650 to $1,200.

candidates.name: Danielle Ford
candidates.ballotNote: Nonpartisan candidate who qualified for the ballot by gathering 250 valid signatures.
candidates.currentRole: Member, Nevada State Board of Education

priorities.text: Reform education spending, including state procurement of outside education contracts.
priorities.quote: strengthen our procurement laws around spending, but specifically education spending

priorities.text: Says she wants to be "the education governor," and would replace standardized tests with teacher updates to parents.
Says Las Vegas does not need more data centers at this point, and that the state should set a plan for artificial intelligence first.

candidates.researchNotes: Her campaign site (daniellefornevada.com) blocked automated access, so it was not read; statements come from a KTNV interview. BallotReady lists issue headings for her but its text is not in her own words, so it was not used. No stance found on the other listed issues.

statements.quote: So we need to make attainable housing with what we have
statements.context: In a KTNV interview, on housing

researchNotes: Nevada elects its lieutenant governor separately, so no running mates are noted. The Nevada Secretary of State's own candidate list is behind a bot-protection wall (not bypassed). The slate was confirmed against Clark County's official Notice of General Election for Nov. 3, 2026, which lists Aaron D. Ford (DEM), Danielle Ford (NPP, no political party), Joseph Lombardo (REP) and 'None of these candidates' for governor; it also matches Vote Clock's reproduction of the Secretary of State's certified list (dated Aug. 25, 2026), Wikipedia and The Nevada Independent's voter guide, which list only Lombardo (R), Aaron Ford (D) and Danielle Ford (no party) for governor. BallotReady's listing also shows the same three; no Libertarian or Independent American candidate is listed for governor. Lombardo's veto and bill-signing figures are from his office's June 2025 statement.
